questions.stem: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two parents who are both carriers (Ff) have a child. What is the probability that the child will be a carrier of cystic fibrosis but NOT affected?
questions.explanation: From Ff x Ff, the Punnett square gives: FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Carriers are Ff - they have one copy of the recessive allele but do not show symptoms because the dominant allele masks it. There are 2 Ff out of 4 possible outcomes, so the probability of being a carrier (but unaffected) is 2/4 = 1/2 (50%).

questions.stem: Polydactyly (extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele (D). A father with polydactyly (Dd) and an unaffected mother (dd) have children. What proportion of their children would be expected to have polydactyly?
questions.explanation: Crossing Dd x dd gives: Dd, Dd, dd, dd. Since polydactyly is dominant, offspring with Dd will be affected and those with dd will not. That gives 2/4 = 1/2 (50%) affected. Unlike recessive disorders where both parents must be carriers, dominant disorders can be passed on by just one affected parent.

questions.stem: A genetic counsellor tells a couple that they are both carriers of sickle cell disease. The couple already has one unaffected child. What is the probability that their second child will have sickle cell disease?

options.text: 0%, because the first child was unaffected
50%, because one parent must pass on the sickle cell allele
75%, because the probability increases with each child

questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is recessive. Both parents are carriers (Hh x Hh). Each child independently has a 1/4 (25%) chance of being hh (affected), 2/4 chance of being Hh (carrier), and 1/4 chance of being HH (unaffected non-carrier). The outcome of the first pregnancy has no influence on the second.

questions.stem: A couple considers genetic screening before having children. Embryonic screening could tell them if an embryo has cystic fibrosis. Which is a valid ethical concern about embryonic screening?

options.text: The screening process changes the DNA of the embryo
It could lead to selecting embryos based on non-medical traits, raising concerns about 'designer babies'
Screened embryos always develop normally with no genetic disorders
Genetic screening is too inaccurate to be useful

questions.explanation: A major ethical concern is that the technology used to screen for serious genetic disorders could be extended to select embryos based on non-medical characteristics (such as sex, eye colour, or intelligence), leading to so-called 'designer babies.' Screening does not alter DNA (that would be gene therapy). The accuracy of modern screening is generally very high.

questions.stem: Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele. A person with one affected parent (Hh) and one unaffected parent (hh) is worried about developing the disease. If they have NOT inherited the allele, can they pass the disease to their children?

options.text: Yes, because the disease can skip a generation
Yes, because all children of an affected grandparent are at risk
No, if they are hh they do not carry the allele and cannot pass it on
No, but they could still develop symptoms later in life

questions.explanation: If the person's genotype is hh (they did not inherit the dominant H allele), they do not have the disease and cannot pass it to their children. Dominant conditions do not skip generations - if you do not have the allele, you cannot pass it on. A genetic test could confirm whether they are Hh (will develop the disease) or hh (unaffected and not a carrier).
